new_statements.translation: 2.1.2. Stress in the classical sense is absent in Guro; however, under the effect of reduction a metrical inequality of syllables is developing. Depending on the structure, in a disyllabic foot either the first syllable may be weakened (up to loss of the first vowel) or the second (up to loss of the initial consonant of the second syllable): tẹ́lẹ́ > tlẹ́ 'earth' ... (in southern dialects) lāwà > lāà 'pocket', pálụ́ > páụ́ 'baldness', or neither. These phenomena have no phonological significance, but in the long run the process may lead to the development of word and syntagmatic stress. Within the syntagm the rhythmic peak (the syntactic head word, or the last word of the group) is also phonetically marked by intensity and vowel duration.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Guro is a tone language (5 tonemes: H, M, L, rising, falling; TBU = syllable) with no word stress in the classical sense. Within the (maximally disyllabic) phonological foot there is structure-dependent, non-contrastive weakening of one syllable: in CVLV feet with identical vowels the first vowel reduces/deletes (CLV), in some CVV/CVLV feet with unlike vowels the second syllable weakens, and some feet show neither; the authors treat this as phonetic, predictable from segmental make-up, and not (yet) stress. Vydrine 2003 analysed the same facts as a 'dynamic accent' falling on the second syllable of CVLV feet in the great majority of cases and on the first when V1 is more open than V2, with a residual 'accentless' class; Kuznetsova 2007 and Kuznetsova & Kuznetsova 2017 explicitly reject a phonological accent.
new_statements.exceptions: Feet meeting CVLV criteria that resist reduction (ɓēlē 'comme', túlú 'tôt'); southern dialects reduce less and show second-syllable consonant loss (lāwà > lāà); Vydrine 2003 lists 'accentless' feet with roughly equal vowels (lólú 'brouillard', lílí, kṵ̀nṵ̄) and words where intensity and length split between the two vowels.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain of the syllable-inequality is the phonological foot (pied/стопа), a unit between syllable and word; phrase level: rhythmic peak of the syntagm (head or last word) marked by intensity and duration. Description based on the Zuénoula (central) dialect zone; lexical citation forms.
new_statements.identity_note: All three primary sources describe the Zuénoula (central) dialect zone of Guro (Kuznetsovas' fieldwork with Zuénoula-dialect speakers; Vydrine's informants from Gaïzra/Zuénoula, parlers mʌ and maa); the 2017 chapter notes southern dialects reduce feet less and differently. Language-level glottocode guro1248 applies; no separate dialect glottocode assigned here.

new_statements.quote: A mon avis, la notion d'accent phonologique n'est pas très fonctionnelle pour le gouro, au moins au stade actuel de son évolution. D'abord, la réduction d'une syllabe est prévisible à partir de la structure segmentale de la séquence. C'est-à-dire que des paires minimales se distinguant par l'accent ne sont pas possibles. [...] Cependant, il est important de noter qu'une inégalité hiérarchique phonologique entre les syllabes est en train de se créer en gouro dans le cadre du pied, mais aussi dans le groupe rythmique auquel le pied sert de base. Il s'agit d'un phénomène du niveau phonétique qui ressemble à l'accent lexical et syntagmatique.
new_statements.translation: In my view, the notion of phonological accent is not very functional for Guro, at least at the present stage of its evolution. First, the reduction of a syllable is predictable from the segmental structure of the sequence. That is, minimal pairs distinguished by accent are not possible. [...] However, it is important to note that a hierarchical phonological inequality between syllables is in the process of forming in Guro within the foot, and also within the rhythmic group of which the foot is the base. This is a phonetic-level phenomenon that resembles lexical and phrasal accent.

new_statements.relation_note: Same authors and same position as the existing statement from Kuznetsova & Kuznetsova 2017 (Jazyki mira: 'Ударение в классическом смысле в Г.я. отсутствует, однако под действием редукции развивается метрическая неравноправность слогов'). Refines it by giving the argument: reduction is predictable from segmental structure, hence no minimal pairs, hence no phonological accent; and by naming the position it rejects (Vydrine 2002, 2003).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Guro is a tone language (three level tonemes in complementary distribution plus a modulated tone, sec. 1). Kuznetsova rejects a phonological word accent: syllable reduction inside the disyllabic foot is predictable from the segmental make-up of the sequence, so accent can never distinguish words; outside prototypical feet the reduction is weak and unstable (p. 41). What exists is an emerging, phonetic-level inequality of syllables within the foot and the rhythmic group, which only resembles lexical/phrasal accent. She explicitly answers Vydrine 2002/2003, who had posited a dynamic accent (p. 41: 'Les modèles différents de la réduction ont amené Vydrine à supposer l'existence de l'accent en gouro'). Data: young speakers of the Zuénoula dialect (fn. 3, p. 13).
new_statements.exceptions: none stated; reduction is described as weak and unstable outside prototypical feet (p. 41)
new_statements.identity_note: Kuznetsova 2007 describes the speech of young speakers of the Zuénoula dialect (fn. 3, p. 13). Vydrine 2003 works with informant Doubi Benjamin (p. 112) and compares Le Saout's and Benoist's recordings; he mentions possible dialectal variants for some tonal realisations but does not tie the accent observations to a named dialect. The listed work (Mandenkan 43: 47-59) is about Mwan (mwan1250), a different South Mande language.

new_statements.quote: 3. L'autre divergence concerne l'existence en gouro d'un accent dynamique, ignorée dans la description de Le Saout [...]. Dans les « pieds » dissyllabiques à voyelles identiques (type CVLV), c'est la deuxième syllabe qui porte l'accent dans la grande majorité des cas (d'où la réduction de la première voyelle, parfois jusqu'à son élimination compete). Dans les « pieds » à voyelles différentes, l'emplacement de l'accent varie d'un mot à l'autre, et la voyelle non accentuée est le plus souvent réduite. Il semble que la première voyelle tend à être accentuée quand elle est plus ouverte que la deuxième, la deuxième voyelle étant accentuée dans tous les autres cas.
new_statements.translation: 3. The other divergence concerns the existence in Guro of a dynamic accent, ignored in Le Saout's description [...]. In disyllabic 'feet' with identical vowels (type CVLV), it is the second syllable that carries the accent in the great majority of cases (hence the reduction of the first vowel, sometimes to its complete elimination). In 'feet' with different vowels, the position of the accent varies from word to word, and the unaccented vowel is most often reduced. It seems that the first vowel tends to be accented when it is more open than the second, the second vowel being accented in all other cases.

new_statements.relation_note: Vydrine posits a word-level dynamic accent with partly predictable placement, whereas the catalog's existing statement (Kuznetsova & Kuznetsova 2017) and Kuznetsova 2007 say stress in the classical sense is absent and the syllable inequality is a phonetic effect of reduction. The disagreement is largely one of status (phonological accent vs. predictable phonetic prominence): both describe the same second-syllable prominence in CVLV feet and the same vowel-openness effect. Vydrine himself labels his account preliminary, and Kuznetsova 2007 p. 41 rebuts it explicitly.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Guro has tone (three level tonemes, p. 112) and, according to Vydrine, additionally a dynamic accent (intensity plus vowel length) within the disyllabic foot, offered as 'observations préliminaires' (p. 91). Placement: in CVLV feet with identical vowels the second syllable is accented and the first vowel reduces; in feet with different vowels the first vowel is accented when it is more open than the second, otherwise the second. Conclusions p. 112: 'le gouro a, à côté du ton, un accent dynamique dont l'emplacement est partiellement déterminé par les types des combinaisons vocaliques à l'intérieur du « pied ». Un « pied » dissyllabique peut porter l'accent sur la première syllabe, sur la deuxième syllabe, ou ne pas avoir d'accent'. The accented syllable also carries the main part of the tonal contour (p. 91).
new_statements.secondary_stress: none stated; phrase-level accent noted: in e miania 'il dépasse' the dynamic accent falls on the pronoun without reducing the verb's vowels; relation between phrase and word accent left for future study (p. 92)
new_statements.exceptions: a third class of feet where the first vowel is louder but the second is not reduced (lolu 'brouillard', lili, kunu, mwene) and words where force and length split between the two vowels; provisionally treated as 'mots sans accent' (p. 92)
new_statements.identity_note: Kuznetsova 2007 describes the speech of young speakers of the Zuénoula dialect (fn. 3, p. 13). Vydrine 2003 works with informant Doubi Benjamin (p. 112) and compares Le Saout's and Benoist's recordings; he mentions possible dialectal variants for some tonal realisations but does not tie the accent observations to a named dialect. The listed work (Mandenkan 43: 47-59) is about Mwan (mwan1250), a different South Mande language.

readall_conflicts: Vydrine 2003 (Mandenkan 38: 91-92, 112) posits a dynamic accent alongside tone, second-syllable in CVLV feet and openness-driven elsewhere, with a class of accentless words; Kuznetsova 2007 (Mandenkan 43: 41) answers him directly: reduction is predictable from segmental structure, no minimal pairs by accent, so 'la notion d'accent phonologique n'est pas très fonctionnelle pour le gouro', only a phonetic-level inequality of syllables that resembles accent. Kuznetsova & Kuznetsova 2017 (the catalog's existing statement) restate the 2007 position. The listed Perekhvalskaya item is not a third voice: it is a mis-citation and is about Mwan. The disagreement is about phonological status, not about which syllable is prominent.

sources.note: Sec. 3 and Conclusions: argues Guro has, besides tone, a dynamic accent (intensity + vowel length) ignored by Le Saout and all earlier descriptions; in CVLV feet with identical vowels the second syllable carries the accent in the great majority of cases (first vowel reduced, sometimes deleted); with different vowels placement varies word to word, first vowel tending to be accented when more open than the second, otherwise the second; a third group of 'accentless' feet; placement 'partiellement déterminé' by vowel combinations; phrase accent unstudied. Explicitly preliminary.
